source_text: Ex quibus ergo Anima corporis expers ostenditur, ex iis potissimum etiam simplex demonstratur. Nam si corpus non est, et omne corpus compositum est; compositum autem ex partibus constet, nec plurium quidem partium erit. Cum autem incorporea sit, simplex erit: quoniam non est composita, neque in partes secabilis.
thought_title: The soul is shown to be simple because it is incorporeal
orientation: Gregory concludes the previous demonstration that the soul is not a body but incorporeal, and now argues from that result that the soul must also be simple.
pass_a_gloss: From which things therefore the soul is shown to be without body, from those things especially also it is demonstrated to be simple. For if it is not a body, and every body is composite; but the composite consists of parts, nor will it be of many parts indeed. Since however it is incorporeal, it will be simple: because it is not composite, nor divisible into parts.

choices.why: Literal rendering of the genitive + adjective construction; matches the glossary's 'incorporeal' sense but here the Latin says 'lacking body' rather than using the single adjective 'incorporea'.
Preserves the emphatic 'potissimum' (especially / most of all) which marks the logical priority of the same arguments.

choices.english: nor will it be of many parts indeed
choices.why: 'Quinde' adds emphasis ('indeed'); 'erit' is future 'will be' referring to the hypothetical composite nature.
rejected: nor will it be of many parts
nor is it of many parts

choices.why: Literal sense of the passive adjective 'secabilis' with 'in partes'; avoids the more abstract 'separable'.
rejected: able to be cut into parts

pass_b_english: From those arguments the soul is shown to be without body; from them especially it is also demonstrated to be simple. For if the soul is not a body, and every body is composite, and a composite thing consists of parts, then the soul will not be composed of many parts. Since the soul is incorporeal, it will be simple: because it is not composite, nor divisible into parts.

problems.quote: then a composite thing consists of parts — yet the soul will not be composed of many parts
problems.source_quote: Nam si corpus non est, et omne corpus compositum est; compositum autem ex partibus constet, nec plurium quidem partium erit.
problems.why: That a composite consists of parts is a further premise, not the consequence. The apodosis is that the soul will not be of many parts.
problems.fix: For if the soul is not a body, and every body is composite, and a composite consists of parts, then the soul will not be of many parts.
problems.ruling: "Nam si... et omne corpus compositum est; compositum autem ex partibus constet" are all premises; only "nec plurium... partium erit" is the apodosis. The English adds "then" and "yet", which garbles the argument.

edits.old: For if the soul is not a body, and every body is composite, then a composite thing consists of parts — yet the soul will not be composed of many parts.
edits.new: For if the soul is not a body, and every body is composite, and a composite thing consists of parts, then the soul will not be composed of many parts.

fixed: Fixed the logical structure of the conditional: the Latin 'compositum autem ex partibus constet' is a further premise (and a composite consists of parts), not the apodosis. The apodosis is 'nec plurium quidem partium erit' (it will not be of many parts). The English now reads as a single conditional chain matching the source.
